# Purchase mechanics for a US non-resident

Covers who may buy, what permit applies, and which authority issues it. Sources
in [citations.md](../citations.md).

## Summary

| Country | May a US citizen acquire | Instrument | Authority | Evidence |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Hungary | Yes, **with a discretionary permit** | Act LXXVIII of 1993 § 1/A(2); Decree 251/2014 | County or Budapest government office | [3][4] |
| Mexico — inland | Yes, permit deemed granted on silence | LIE Art. 10 A | SRE | [5][6] |
| Mexico — restricted zone | **Not by direct title.** 50-year bank trust | LIE Arts. 11–13 | SRE + credit institution | [5][6] |
| Costa Rica — coastal 200 m | **No** for a non-resident | Ley 6043 Art. 47 | Municipality (concession) | [7] |
| Costa Rica — inland titled land | Not established | — | — | gap |
| Italy | **Unresolved** — reciprocity applies, US answer not obtained | Art. 16 preleggi (R.D. 262/1942) | Notary verifies | [1][2] |
| France, Spain, Portugal, Greece, Panama | Not established | — | — | gap |

## Hungary — the clearest documented gate, and it is closed to a US buyer by default

Act LXXVIII of 1993 § 1/A(2), quoted in the government-office guidance [3]:

> "külföldi jogi vagy külföldi természetes személy, a mező- és erdőgazdasági
> földnek nem minősülő ingatlan tulajdonjogát, az ingatlan fekvése szerint
> illetékes fővárosi és vármegyei kormányhivatal engedélyével szerezheti meg"

A foreign natural or legal person may acquire title to non-agricultural,
non-forestry property **only with the permission of the government office** for
the property's location. The exemption list is exhaustive — EU and EEA
nationals, Swiss nationals, dual nationals with a Hungarian or EU nationality,
inheritance, refugees, certain Withdrawal Agreement UK nationals — and **the
United States is not on it**. The guidance closes the point explicitly: the
permit is required "regardless of what status (e.g. settled, immigrant)" the
applicant holds in Hungary [3].

Mechanics [3][4]:

- **Fee: HUF 65,000 per property** (§ 1/B(1)). The reduced HUF 13,000 fee is for
  free-movement or settled persons who have initiated Hungarian naturalisation,
  so it does not reach a US non-resident. The two government sheets state the
  reduced-fee condition slightly differently ("letelepedett jogállású" in [3],
  "huzamos tartózkodási jogosultsággal rendelkező" in [4]); the discrepancy does
  not affect a US buyer.
- **Decision deadline: 45 days**, attributed by [4] to § 3 of Decree 251/2014.
  If the authority misses it, it must refund an amount equal to the fee.
- The office **must consult the local municipality** on municipal interest, and
  for natural persons must query the aliens-policing directorate and the
  national police on public-interest grounds.
- **Refusal is mandatory** where the acquisition harms public or municipal
  interest. Remedy is an administrative lawsuit within 30 days.

This is a per-property, discretionary permit with a local-interest veto. It is a
timeline and execution risk to be priced, not a bar.

## Mexico — two different risk classes that must not be flattened

The restricted zone is defined in the statute [5], Art. 2 fr. VI: "cien
kilómetros a lo largo de las fronteras y de cincuenta a lo largo de las playas"
— **100 km along borders, 50 km along coasts**.

**Inland.** Art. 10 A: the foreigner files the Calvo-clause undertaking with SRE
and obtains a permit, which is **deemed granted** if SRE does not publish a
refusal in the DOF within 5 business days (municipality wholly outside the
zone), or 30 business days where the municipality is partly inside [5].

**Inside the restricted zone, residential use.** Direct title is unavailable.
Art. 11 permits a credit institution to acquire, as trustee, rights over the
property "cuando el objeto del fideicomiso sea permitir la utilización y el
aprovechamiento de tales bienes **sin constituir derechos reales sobre ellos**"
[5]. The foreign beneficiary holds use and enjoyment, expressly **not rights in
rem**. Art. 12 confirms rental income is within the permitted scope. Art. 13
sets a **50-year maximum term, extendable on application** — permissive, not
guaranteed. Art. 14 states the SRE decides "considerando el beneficio económico
y social que la realización de estas operaciones implique para la Nación", a
discretionary public-interest standard.

Art. 38 fr. V penalises simulated acts to let a foreigner enjoy restricted-zone
property "con multa hasta por el importe de la operación" — a fine up to the
whole purchase price [5]. That is the exposure attached to nominee and
corporate workarounds.

**Currency caveat.** The SRE trámite page [6] confirms the process is running,
but is stamped 2 October 2020 and records that a SIPAC27 system failure led SRE
to **suspend the 5-business-day statutory deadline** under a DOF accord of 29
September 2020. Whether that suspension persists is not established.

## Costa Rica — a bar, not a permit, on the coast

Ley 6043 [7] makes the 200 m maritime-terrestrial zone "parte del patrimonio
nacional… inalienable e imprescriptible" (Art. 1), splits it into a 50 m public
zone that "no puede ser objeto de ocupación bajo ningún título" (Arts. 10, 20)
and a 150 m restricted zone where only municipal **concessions** are available
(Arts. 39–41), for 5 to 20 years (Art. 48).

Art. 47, quoted in full because it is decisive:

> "No se otorgarán concesiones: a) A extranjeros que no hayan residido en el
> país por lo menos durante cinco años; b) A sociedades anónimas con acciones al
> portador; c) A sociedades o entidades domiciliadas en el exterior; ch) A
> entidades constituidas en el país por extranjeros; y d) A entidades cuyas
> acciones o cuotas o capital, correspondan en más de cincuenta por ciento a
> extranjeros."

Share transfers to foreigners in breach "carecerán de toda validez". A US
non-resident is caught by (a) and by (c)/(d) for the obvious workarounds. For
islands the position is worse: Art. 10 places the entire remaining land of an
island in the restricted zone.

**What this does not say.** Ley 6043 Art. 6 excludes registered private property
and coastal-city areas from its own scope, which implies an ordinary titled-land
regime exists alongside — but no fetched source describes it. **The general rule
for inland Costa Rican property is a gap**, caused by an SSL failure on the
national legal database and the loss of the Investment Climate Statements [63].

## Italy — the gate is documented, the answer is not

MAECI [1] states the rule verbatim: under Art. 16 of the General Law Provisions
(R.D. 262 of 16 March 1942), "Foreigners are admitted to enjoy the civil rights
attributed to citizens on condition of reciprocity". Ownership rights in
immovable property are expressly within the covered investment forms. The
exemption list — EU/EEA nationals, non-EU nationals resident in Italy with a
qualifying permit, stateless persons and refugees resident three years — **does
not cover a non-resident US buyer**.

MAECI also states the escape route: verification "should not be carried out for
nationals of the countries with which Italy has concluded Bilateral Investment
Treaties (BITs)", the ratifying instrument being *lex specialis* to Art. 16 [1].

**The page never mentions the United States.** The per-country determination
lives on the linked *Elenco Paesi e territori*, which is bot-blocked to this
run's retrieval path [2], as is the Italian-language mirror of [1].

**But a treaty instrument was retrieved, and it speaks directly to property.**
The Italian ratification of the US–Italy Treaty of Friendship, Commerce and
Navigation, Law 385 of 18 June 1949, Art. VII(1) [8], provides:

> "I Cittadini e le persone giuridiche ed associazioni di ciascuna Alta Parte
> Contraente avranno facoltà di acquistare possedere e disporre di **beni
> immobili o di altri diritti reali** nei territori dell'altra Alta Parte
> Contraente alle seguenti condizioni: … b) nel caso di cittadini e di persone
> giuridiche ed associazioni degli Stati Uniti d'America, il diritto di
> acquistare, possedere e disporre di tali beni e diritti sarà **a condizioni non
> meno favorevoli di quelle accordate o che potranno essere accordate in avvenire
> ai cittadini e alle persone giuridiche ed associazioni della Repubblica
> italiana**"

That is a **national-treatment guarantee on immovable property**, expressly for
US citizens and legal persons: conditions no less favourable than those granted
to Italians. The reciprocal limb (a) makes the Italian right in the US depend on
the law of the state where the property sits — the conditional structure typical
of these instruments.

**What is established, and what is not.** The treaty text grants the right; MAECI
states that reciprocity verification is not carried out where a Bilateral
Investment Treaty exists, the ratifying instrument being *lex specialis* to Art.
16 [1]. What this run **cannot** confirm is whether MAECI treats a 1949 Treaty of
Friendship, Commerce and Navigation as such an instrument for that purpose —
MAECI does not say so on the accessible page, and the country list that would
show it is blocked [2]. An FCN treaty is the historical predecessor of the modern
BIT, not identically named, and the inference is not made here.

So the position is stronger than "unknown" and weaker than "settled": **a treaty
in force grants US citizens national treatment on Italian immovable property
[8], and whether that discharges the Art. 16 reciprocity condition in MAECI's own
administration of it is unconfirmed [1][2].** A notary is the person who must
verify reciprocity before the deed, so this is a question to put to the notary
with the treaty citation in hand rather than one to resolve from public sources.

## Escrow — a hard gap across all nine

A search of the whole fetched corpus for escrow terminology in six languages —
`escrow`, `ügyvédi letét`, `cuenta de plica`, `conto dedicato`, `compte
séquestre`, `deposito fiduciario` — returned **no match for any of the nine
countries**. Nothing is known from this run about how buyer funds are held
between signature and completion, in any jurisdiction studied. That includes the
notary-monopoly countries where the mechanism differs most from US practice.

## Gaps

- **Italy**: the US reciprocity determination (blocked source [2]).
- **France, Spain, Portugal, Greece, Panama**: no source on who may buy.
- **Costa Rica**: the inland titled-land regime.
- **All nine**: escrow and deposit protection; whether a local tax ID is a
  precondition to *execute the deed* as opposed to a precondition to *file tax
  returns*. Spain's NIF is documented as optional on the tax form [38] and
  Mexico's RFC appears only in a rental-phase procedure [40]; neither speaks to
  conveyancing.
